title: Cross-Text Connections
lead: These questions give you two short texts on the same subject and ask how the people in one text would view the ideas in the other: “Based on the texts, how would the researchers in Text 2 most likely respond to the claim in Text 1?” There is twice as much to read, but the two texts are about the same thing, so each one helps you understand the other.

parts.title: Part 1 · Point of view
parts.html:
Every cross-text question is about point of view: what a particular person or group thinks. That person may be the author of a text, or someone named inside it, such as “the theorists” or “Cáceres and colleagues”. The question tells you whose views to compare, so you can read with those people in mind.

Once you know the two points of view, the question is how they relate. Do they agree? Disagree? Does one adjust the other?

Whatever you decide must be supported by the words of the texts. Three kinds of wrong choice come up again and again:

  • Too extreme: the choice makes someone’s opinion stronger than the text does.
  • Swapped: the choice gives one person the view that belongs to the other.
  • Beyond the text: the choice makes a claim about something the texts never discuss.

parts.title: Part 2 · The three-step method
parts.html:
1. Summarize each text. Reduce each one to one or two plain points, with extra attention to what the people in it believe or found. If a text introduces a person, focus on that person’s view. You should finish with one short sentence per text.
  2. Name the relationship. Put your two sentences side by side and say how they connect, in your own words, before you look at the choices.
  3. Test the choices. Pick the one that states the relationship you named. If two still seem possible, drop the one that goes further than the text or exaggerates how strongly someone feels.

parts.title: Part 3 · Worked example: a finding against a theory
parts.html:
Text 1
What factors influence the abundance of species in a given ecological community? Some theorists have argued that historical diversity is a major driver of how diverse an ecological community eventually becomes: differences in community diversity across otherwise similar habitats, in this view, are strongly affected by the number of species living in those habitats at earlier times.

Text 2
In 2010, a group of researchers including biologist Carla Cáceres created artificial pools in a New York forest. They stocked some pools with a diverse mix of zooplankton species and others with a single zooplankton species and allowed the pool communities to develop naturally thereafter. Over the course of four years, Cáceres and colleagues periodically measured the species diversity of the pools, finding—contrary to their expectations—that by the end of the study there was little to no difference in the pools’ species diversity. Based on the texts, how would Cáceres and colleagues (Text 2) most likely describe the view of the theorists presented in Text 1?
A) It is largely correct, but it requires a minor refinement in light of the research team’s results.
B) It is not compelling as a theory regardless of any experimental data collected by the research team.
C) It may seem plausible, but it is not supported by the research team’s findings.
D) It probably holds true only in conditions like those in the research team’s study.

Summarize. Text 1: theorists say that more species at the start leads to more species later. Text 2: researchers started some pools with many species and some with one, and after four years the pools were about equally diverse, which surprised them.

Name the relationship. Disagreement. The experiment did not show what the theory predicts.

Test the choices.

  • D says the theory holds in conditions like the study’s. The study found the opposite.
  • B says the researchers found the theory unconvincing whatever the data showed. The text says the result was “contrary to their expectations”, so they expected the theory to hold. This goes beyond the text.
  • A calls the theory “largely correct” with a small adjustment. The result contradicts the theory outright, so this is too mild.
  • C fits both halves: the theory sounded reasonable (the researchers expected it), and their findings did not support it. C is the answer.

parts.title: Part 4 · The relationships you will meet
parts.html:
Agree and disagree are the two ends. Most hard questions sit between them.

RelationshipWhat Text 2 doesTypical wording in the answer
AgreementSupports or confirms Text 1’s claim“is consistent with”, “provides support for”
DisagreementRejects or contradicts the claim“is not supported by”, “challenges”
QualificationAgrees, but adds a limit or condition“is largely correct but”, “holds only when”
Same evidence, different explanationAccepts the finding and explains it another way“offers an alternative explanation for”
ExtensionBuilds on the claim or applies it to a new case“elaborates on”, “builds on”

A qualification is not a rejection. If Text 2 says a finding is real but limited, that is agreement with a caveat. Seeing “however” in Text 2 is not enough to choose “disputes”; read what the rest of the sentence does.

A shared topic is not agreement. Two texts can be about the same fossil or the same study and reach opposite conclusions. Decide from the claims, never from the topic.

Check the direction. “How would the researchers in Text 2 respond to Text 1?” is a different question from the reverse. Note who is responding to whom before you read the choices.

parts.title: Part 5 · Tips that save points
parts.html:
TipHow to use it
Look for + and −Words with a positive or negative charge show how someone feels about an idea: “compelling”, “flawed”, “surprisingly”, “fails to”. A positive attitude in one text and a negative one in the other points to disagreement.
Stick to the textDo not guess what an author would probably think about something the text does not mention. Wrong choices are often too strong or cover cases the texts never raise.
Follow the transitionsWords like however, because and therefore mark where a view turns or where a conclusion arrives. The conclusion of each text is usually what you need to compare.

The reading habits from Class 1 apply here too: strip the details, do not stall on a hard word, shorten the jargon, and eliminate before you guess.

parts.title: Part 6 · Worked example: an understandable mistake
parts.html:
Text 1
A tiny, unusual fossil in a piece of 99-million-year-old amber is of the extinct species Oculudentavis khaungraae. The O. khaungraae fossil consists of a rounded skull with a thin snout and a large eye socket. Because these features look like they are avian, or related to birds, researchers initially thought that the fossil might be the smallest avian dinosaur ever found.

Text 2
Paleontologists were excited to discover a second small fossil that is similar to the strange O. khaungraae fossil but has part of the lower body along with a birdlike skull. Detailed studies of both fossils revealed several traits that are found in lizards but not in dinosaurs or birds. Therefore, paleontologists think the two creatures were probably unusual lizards, even though the skulls looked avian at first. Based on the texts, what would the paleontologists in Text 2 most likely say about the researchers’ initial thought in Text 1?
A) It is understandable because the fossil does look like it could be related to birds, even though O. khaungraae is probably a lizard.
B) It is confusing because it isn’t clear what caused the researchers to think that O. khaungraae might be related to birds.
C) It is flawed because the researchers mistakenly assumed that O. khaungraae must be a lizard.
D) It is reasonable because the O. khaungraae skull is about the same size as the skull of the second fossil but is shaped differently.

Shorten the jargon and summarize. Call the species “O.K.” Text 1: the O.K. skull looks birdlike, so researchers first thought it was a tiny bird-like dinosaur. Text 2: a second, more complete fossil showed lizard traits, so O.K. was probably a lizard, even though the skull looks birdlike.

Follow the transitions. “Because” in Text 1 and “Therefore” in Text 2 each introduce a conclusion: bird-like dinosaur in Text 1, lizard in Text 2. Those two conclusions are what the question compares.

Name the relationship. Text 2 corrects Text 1 but grants its starting point: the skull really does look birdlike. That is a qualification, not a flat rejection.

Test the choices.

  • B says it is unclear why the researchers thought of birds. Text 1 gives the reason, and Text 2 repeats it.
  • C swaps the views. The Text 1 researchers thought “bird”, not “lizard”.
  • D gives a reason about skull size and shape that neither text mentions, and Text 2 calls the fossils similar.
  • A matches: the first idea made sense given how the skull looks, and the creature is probably a lizard. A is the answer.

parts.title: Part 7 · Write it down, then check the charge
parts.html:
Two short texts on an unfamiliar subject are a lot to hold in your head. Handle as little as possible at a time, and put it on scratch paper.

  1. Text 1: main point, in a few words.
  2. Text 2: main point, in a few words.
  3. The relationship: agree (+), disagree (−), or agree with a limit (±).
  4. Your own answer to the question.
  5. The choice closest to it.

After step 3 the question is mostly answered before you have read a single choice.

The first words of a choice carry its charge. If Text 2 disagrees with Text 1, cross out every choice that opens with approval, and the reverse.

A choice that begins…Charge
“It is well supported by…”, “It is consistent with…”+
“It overlooks…”, “It overstates…”, “It is unconvincing because…”−
“It is largely accurate but…”, “It holds only when…”±

Agreement on one point, disagreement on another. Two texts that disagree overall can still share a starting fact. A correct choice may say both: “They agree that the fossils are old but differ on what they show.”

Example.
Text 1. Some historians argue that the printing press spread across fifteenth-century Europe mainly because rulers saw its value and paid for workshops in their capitals.
Text 2. Town records tell a different story. The earliest presses appeared in trading cities with many merchants and few courts, and they were often running for years before any ruler took an interest.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the historians in Text 1? A) By agreeing that rulers' support explains where the first presses appeared
B) By arguing that most merchants of the period could not read
C) By suggesting that the historians give rulers too large a role in the spread of the press
D) By claiming that rulers tried to prevent printing in trading cities Scratch paper: T1: press spread ← rulers. T2: presses first in merchant cities, before rulers cared. Relationship: −.
Charge: A is positive, so it is out.
Text check: B is in neither text. D is negative but goes further than Text 2, which says rulers were late, not hostile.
C is negative and says no more than Text 2 does.

Trap: which text said it? A wrong choice often uses an idea you clearly remember reading, but it comes from the other text. When a choice gives a reason for the response, find that reason in the text of the person who is responding.
